clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: A long, floating vocal line over piano arpeggios that sound like a harp. It feels like a prayer, even though the original words are a German setting of a Walter Scott poem — a girl named Ellen, in the Highlands, asking the Virgin for help.

clues.label: Places the composer lived and worked
clues.text: Almost his whole short life happened in and around one imperial capital. He often didn't even have his own piano — he crashed with friends.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: More than six hundred songs for voice and piano. Almost none of his orchestral music got a public performance while he was alive.

clues.label: A relationship with contemporaries
clues.text: His friends ran regular evening hangouts that were just his music, start to finish. People still use the name they coined for those nights.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: This is the song everyone thinks is a church hymn. Weddings, funerals, talent shows — they all call it Ave Maria. Six hundred songs, dead at thirty-one, and a symphony that stops after two movements. People still call that one the Unfinished.

explanation.summary: The prayer-song everyone already knows, six hundred lieder, and the Unfinished: Franz Schubert, writing Ave Maria in Austria in 1825.

points.text: The Scott setting is Ellens dritter Gesang (Ellen's Third Song), D. 839. Later singers put the Latin Ave Maria under the same tune, which is how most people know it.
The capital is Vienna. Schubert barely left it, and he wrote this song there in 1825.
Six hundred-odd lieder, almost no public orchestral performances. That imbalance is Schubert's career in one line.
Ave Maria plus the Unfinished Symphony plus death at thirty-one. He was a torchbearer at Beethoven's funeral in 1827 and followed him the next year.
